First we would have to restore Goethe’s space and abolish the reality of the human space we live in today.
What was his existential picture of the world?
The concrete answer lies in the line:
That is the concrete sense of space experienced by Goethe the man, at its highest intensity.
But what is the real human space today?
Above our caps, airplanes buzz past—sometimes enemy aircraft, sometimes others.
When we move through space, nearby things rush past quickly. Things farther away move slowly. Eventually the most distant things appear motionless, like fixed stars.
When we move through time, the seconds, minutes, and days of the present seem long to me, while distant periods fly past.
I want to be thought of, I who am entirely thought.
So far, the Song of the Sixty-Year-Old, both as a whole and in its details, has been understood only by people who have themselves physically been inside a prison cell.
In that sense, it belongs under the heading “The Man in the Cell.”
The inner time of the verses is also cell-time—prison-cell time, not monastic-cell time.
Anyone who has never physically known the space of a cell will even misunderstand the word “performance-space.”
Today we are all inside the honeycomb cell of the bee.
Everyone is horrified when their workplace is taken away.
The right to one’s honeycomb cell is treated as a basic right, a right of freedom, a human right.

The present method of turning every literary idea into journalism, of making one’s own correspondence commercially productive, of keeping diaries that are already intended for publication at the moment they are written—all this destroys every good possibility of genuine correspondence.
Instead of a conversation in writing, all we get are scattered and one-sided notes, already glancing sideways at the printing press.
The opposite danger is the transformation of conversation into a chain of causality, in which question and answer become cause and effect. Then all resonance and radiation stop.
I am the messenger in the chain, a messenger am I in the chain.
(Pro quo legatione fungor in catena, ὑπὲρ οὗ πρεσβεύω ἐν ἁλύσει)
(The end of the Letter to the Ephesians, Eph. 6:20.)

Gottfried Benn’s letter, which moved us so deeply when we read it in manuscript several months ago, has now been published in issue 12 of Merkur. And look what happens: licensed publicity destroys everything.
The questionnaire is not some Balkan invention. It is a Bolshevik-American invention.
There was something in the manuscript of Benn’s letter that I barely noticed and paid no attention to at all.
Now that the letter has been printed unchanged, this one thing suddenly stands at the center of everything, illuminating everything, putting everything in its true light, dominating the whole text:
Probably even the American questionnaire with its 143 questions, each to be answered yes or no.
Whose questionnaire is actually in order today?
Answer: That of the nihilist Gottfried Benn!
At last, a questionnaire that is in order—even the questionnaire of a German nihilist who has been publishing books for more than thirty years!
Or are they perhaps such superior virtuosos in obeying the enemy’s legality?

“products of an authoritarian barracks culture that wanted to breed herd animals and cannon fodder for large-space politics, while filling the emptiness of its leading personalities and the vacuum of its intellectual world with the hysterical screaming of psychopaths and the cult of violence that has always given weaklings their rigid military bearing.”
The hysteria of the small space sounds just as shrill as the arrogance of the large space.
The spirit of the person being insulted immediately enters the person doing the insulting. That is what now fills the intellectual space.
How the mill clatters beside the rushing stream!
No one speaks a true word anymore.
What am I doing if I publish the Donoso essay anonymously?
Am I doing with my legitimate child what Rousseau did with his illegitimate ones when he left his newborn children at the door of the foundling hospital?

I am merely removing a conspicuous badge from the child’s coat so as not to provoke the fury of its enemies. I take off its red headscarf because we are passing close to enraged bulls. That does not mean I deny my child or abandon it. I am simply behaving as the situation requires. For the first principle of a good father is also:
Being incorruptible is not much; being impossible to deceive is the goal.

The anti-fascist concept of the “victim”: not so much a substitute for religion, or a substitute religion, but rather a substitute morality.
A moral foundation for receiving privileges while standing in line and when jobs are being handed out.
A moral justification for elbowing better-qualified competitors out of the way under a manipulated system of legality.

Prohibition of alcohol as a form of hostility toward the Catholic sacrament of the altar.
